prompt: A library maintains information about BOOKS and PUBLISHERS. The business rules state: every book is published by exactly one publisher; a publisher may publish many books or none. Which cardinality constraint best describes this relationship?

options.text: Many-to-one from BOOK to PUBLISHER, with mandatory participation for PUBLISHER
One-to-one between BOOK and PUBLISHER
Many-to-many between BOOK and PUBLISHER
One-to-many from PUBLISHER to BOOK, with optional participation for PUBLISHER

explanation: Two things are being asked at once, so answer them separately. Cardinality: one publisher to many books, so one-to-many from PUBLISHER to BOOK. Participation: the words OR NONE mean a publisher need not appear at all, so PUBLISHER is optional. Only one option gets both right, and the trap option gets the cardinality right and the participation backwards.

why.a: Wrong on participation, and that is the whole trap. The phrase or none makes PUBLISHER optional, not mandatory.
why.b: Wrong. One-to-one would stop a publisher having many books.
why.c: Wrong. Many-to-many would need a book to have several publishers, and the rule says exactly one.
why.d: Correct. One-to-many from publisher to book, and optional for publisher because of or none.

prompt: In a database, who or what typically provides the source for establishing business rules?

options.text: The default configuration settings of the relational database management system (RDBMS).
Managers, policy makers, and operational procedures within an organization.
The network architecture and router configurations.
Standard open-source libraries downloaded from the internet.

explanation: Business rules come from the BUSINESS, which means the people who run it and the procedures they follow. That is why gathering requirements is interviewing, not reading a manual. Every cardinality and participation constraint on this paper began life as somebody in an organisation saying every patient must have a doctor.

why.a: Wrong, and backwards: the DBMS is configured to enforce the rules, it does not invent them.
why.b: Correct. Managers, policy makers and operational procedures.
why.c: Wrong. Network hardware is infrastructure and has no view on how the business works.
why.d: Wrong. A library is code somebody else wrote, not a statement of your organisation's policy.

prompt: What does an "Entity" represent in an Entity-Relationship Model?

options.text: A specific physical hard drive sector where data resides.
The software interface used to log into a database.
A person, place, object, event, or concept in the real world about which data is captured.
A specific database query execution plan.

explanation: Person, place, object, event or concept. Learn that list as a list, because it is quoted in the definition and because it is what tells you an ACCOUNT and a BOOKING are entities as surely as a STUDENT is. The test for whether something belongs in your model is simple: does the organisation need to keep data about it?

why.a: Wrong. Sectors are physical storage, which the conceptual model deliberately ignores.
why.b: Wrong. That is an application, not something you keep data about.
why.c: Correct. Person, place, object, event or concept.
why.d: Wrong. An execution plan is how the DBMS answers a query, an internal matter.

prompt: An online shopping system maintains CUSTOMERS and ORDERS. The business rules state: a customer may place many orders or none; every order must be placed by exactly one customer. Which relationship should be represented in the ER diagram?

options.text: One-to-one relationship between CUSTOMER and ORDER
Many-to-many relationship between CUSTOMER and ORDER
Unary relationship on CUSTOMER
One-to-many relationship from CUSTOMER to ORDER with optional participation for CUSTOMER

explanation: Same two-part method as the publisher question. Cardinality: many orders per customer, one customer per order, so one-to-many from CUSTOMER to ORDER. Participation: OR NONE again, so CUSTOMER is optional. Notice the examiner reuses one phrasing across several questions, which means learning to spot or none is worth several marks on its own.

why.a: Wrong. One-to-one would stop a customer placing more than one order.
why.b: Wrong. Many-to-many would need an order to belong to several customers, and the rule says exactly one.
why.c: Wrong. Unary means an entity related to itself, and there are two types here.
why.d: Correct. One-to-many from customer to order, optional for customer.

prompt: What is the primary purpose of a business rule in database design?

options.text: To automate the payroll system for database administrators.
To define the precise policies, constraints, and operational principles that the database data must conform to.
To measure the speed of transaction processing in the database engine.
To dictate the pricing strategy of the company's products stored in the database.

explanation: A business rule is a constraint written in English before it is written in a schema. Every employee must belong to exactly one department is a business rule; NOT NULL and a foreign key are how the database enforces it. Rule first, constraint second, and the exam tests the translation between them constantly.

why.a: Wrong. Payroll is an application that might use the database, not a purpose of the rules.
why.b: Correct. The policies, constraints and operational principles the data must conform to.
why.c: Wrong. Speed measurement is performance tuning.
why.d: Wrong. Pricing is a commercial decision; a rule about it would only enter as a constraint on stored values.

prompt: What does a "Relationship" express in an ER model?

options.text: The speed differential between the database and the web server.
The code compatibility between two different SQL dialects.
The synchronization schedule between a primary database and its backup replica.
An association or link between two or more entities.

explanation: An association between entities, and the phrase TWO OR MORE is doing real work: it is what allows ternary relationships. A relationship is usually a verb in the business's own words, teaches, places, is published by, which is why reading the business rules aloud is the fastest way to find them.

why.a: Wrong. Nothing in the conceptual model concerns servers or their speeds.
why.b: Wrong. Dialect differences are an implementation problem.
why.c: Wrong. Replication is an operational concern, not a modelling one.
why.d: Correct. An association or link between two or more entities.

prompt: If a company policy states "Each employee is assigned to exactly one department, and each department can employ many employees," what type of relationship connectivity exists from Department to Employee?

options.text: Many-to-Many (M:N)
One-to-One (1:1)
One-to-Many (1:M)
Many-to-One (M:1)

explanation: The direction is stated, and it decides the answer. FROM Department TO Employee: one department, many employees, so one-to-many. Read it the other way, from employee to department, and the same facts are many-to-one. Same relationship, opposite name, and the only thing that settles it is which end the question starts from. Underline the direction words before you look at the options.

why.a: Wrong. An employee is in exactly one department, so it cannot be many-to-many.
why.b: Wrong. One-to-one would stop a department employing many people.
why.c: Correct. From department to employee is one to many.
why.d: Wrong only because of the direction asked: many-to-one is the same relationship read from Employee to Department.

options.text: An attribute that can be subdivided into smaller, meaningful sub-components.
An attribute that serves as a foreign key to another table.
An attribute whose value is calculated dynamically from other attributes.
An attribute that holds multiple distinct values for a single entity instance.

explanation: ADDRESS is the standard example: it breaks into street, city and postcode, each meaningful on its own. Keep the three attribute types apart by asking one question each. Composite: can I split it? Multivalued: can there be several of them? Derived: is it worked out from something else?

why.a: Correct. It subdivides into smaller meaningful parts, as address does.
why.b: Wrong. That is a foreign key, a relational concept rather than an attribute type.
why.c: Wrong. Calculated from others is DERIVED.
why.d: Wrong. Several values at once is MULTIVALUED, which is the very next question.

prompt: When three distinct entity types participate simultaneously in a single relationship, it is called a:

options.text: Binary relationship
Ternary relationship
Multi-valued relationship
Trilateral relationship

explanation: This is DEGREE again: unary one, binary two, ternary three, and beyond that n-ary. The prefixes are the ordinary Latin ones, the same uni, bi and ter you already know from unicycle, bicycle and tercentenary.

why.a: Wrong. Binary is two entity types, which is the commonest case by far.
why.c: Wrong. Multivalued describes an ATTRIBUTE, not a relationship.
why.d: Wrong. Trilateral is not database vocabulary at all; it is there because it sounds plausible.

prompt: If the minimum cardinality for a relationship is 0, it means that the relationship is:

options.text: Mandatory
Optional
Corrupted
Redundant

explanation: Zero means none is allowed, and being allowed to have none is exactly what optional means. Learn it as a pair: minimum 0 is optional, minimum 1 is mandatory. Every or none in a business rule is a minimum of 0 in disguise.

why.a: Wrong, and it is the other half of the pair: mandatory is a minimum of 1.
why.b: Correct. A minimum of zero means participation is optional.
why.c: Wrong. Corruption is a data integrity failure, not a cardinality.
why.d: Wrong. Redundancy is about duplicated data, a different topic entirely.

prompt: Which type of relationship typically requires a bridge (associative) table to resolve it into a relational database structure?

options.text: One-to-One (1:1)
One-to-Many (1:M)
Unary One-to-One (1:1)
Many-to-Many (M:N)

explanation: A relational table cannot hold many values in one column, so a many-to-many will not fit directly. It is split into two one-to-many relationships around a new table in the middle, called a bridge, associative, junction or link table, holding a foreign key to each side. STUDENT and COURSE become STUDENT, ENROLMENT and COURSE.

why.a: Wrong. One-to-one is implemented by putting a foreign key on either side; no third table is needed.
why.b: Wrong. One-to-many is the natural relational shape: the foreign key goes on the many side.
why.c: Wrong. A unary one-to-one still needs only a foreign key, pointing back at the same table.
why.d: Correct. Many-to-many is the one that must be broken into two one-to-many relationships.

prompt: Which of the following is the best example of a multivalued attribute?

options.text: Employee Monthly Salary
Employee College Degrees (where an employee can have multiple degrees)
Employee Date of Birth
Employee Social Security Number

explanation: Multivalued means several values at once for ONE instance. One employee, one salary, one birth date, one social security number, but possibly three degrees. It is drawn as a double ellipse, and when the model is turned into tables it becomes a table of its own, because a column cannot hold a list.

why.a: Wrong. One employee has one monthly salary at a time, so it is single-valued.
why.b: Correct. One employee can hold several degrees at once.
why.c: Wrong. Everyone has exactly one date of birth.
why.d: Wrong. One number per person, and it is a candidate key at that.

prompt: A relationship between instances of a single entity type is called a:

options.text: Binary relationship
Ternary relationship
Unary (or Recursive) relationship
Quaternary relationship

explanation: One entity type related to itself, which is why it is also called recursive. EMPLOYEE manages EMPLOYEE is the standard case, and so is COURSE is a prerequisite for COURSE. On the diagram it is the relationship whose two lines both run back to the same box.

why.a: Wrong. Binary needs two distinct entity types.
why.c: Correct. One entity type related to itself, also called recursive.
why.d: Wrong. Quaternary would be four entity types.

prompt: A university maintains records of STUDENTS and COURSES. The business rules state: a student may register for many courses or none; every course must have at least one student registered. Which cardinality best represents the relationship between STUDENT and COURSE?

options.text: Many-to-one, with mandatory participation for STUDENT only
One-to-one, with optional participation for both entities
Many-to-many, with optional participation for STUDENT and mandatory participation for COURSE
One-to-many, with mandatory participation for both entities

explanation: Cardinality first: a student takes many courses, and since every course has students registered and courses are shared, it is many-to-many. Participation next: OR NONE makes STUDENT optional, and MUST HAVE AT LEAST ONE makes COURSE mandatory. Note that at least one is the same phrase as a minimum cardinality of 1, said in English.

why.a: Wrong on both counts: the cardinality is not many-to-one, and it is COURSE that is mandatory, not STUDENT.
why.b: Wrong. One-to-one would let a student take only one course.
why.c: Correct. Many-to-many, optional for student, mandatory for course.
why.d: Wrong. Both mandatory contradicts or none, which makes the student side optional.

prompt: In an ER diagram, an attribute that uniquely identifies each entity instance is known as the:

options.text: Derived Key
Foreign Key
Composite Value
Identifier or Primary Key

explanation: UNIQUELY IDENTIFIES is the phrase that always means key. In the conceptual model it is called the identifier and underlined on the diagram; in the relational model it becomes the primary key. It can never be NULL, which ties this question back to the first one on the paper about required attributes.

why.a: Wrong. Derived describes a value computed from others, and no such thing as a derived key is defined here.
why.b: Wrong. A foreign key identifies a row in ANOTHER table; it points outward rather than identifying its own row.
why.c: Wrong. Composite describes an attribute that splits into parts. A composite KEY exists, but composite value is not the term.
why.d: Correct. The identifier, which becomes the primary key.
